stem: In a normally formed heart viewed from the superior aspect, where is the **pulmonary valve** situated relative to the aortic valve?

choices.text: Posterior, inferior and slightly to the right of the aortic valve
Anterior, superior and slightly to the left of the aortic valve
Anterior, inferior and slightly to the right of the aortic valve
Posterior, superior and directly to the left of the aortic valve
Central, wedged between the mitral and tricuspid valves

explanation.text: The **pulmonary valve** lies **anterior, superior and slightly to the left** of the aortic valve; the **aortic valve** is the central valve.

head: Valve
Position (normally formed heart)
rows: ==Central==, wedged between the mitral and tricuspid valves
==Anterior, superior and slightly to the left== of the aortic valve
Anuli merge with each other and the membranous septum -> **fibrous skeleton** of the heart
explanation.caption: Valve interrelationships (Fig. 1.22, superior view)

explanation.text: The interrelationships among the heart valves in normally formed hearts are **remarkably uniform**, so they are reliable landmarks.
"Central, wedged between mitral and tricuspid" describes the **aortic** valve, not the pulmonary valve.
The aortic valve occupies a central position, wedged between the mitral and tricuspid valves, whereas the pulmonary valve is situated anterior, superior, and slightly to the left of the aortic valve

choiceNotes.a: This is the opposite direction; the source places the pulmonary valve **anterior and superior**, slightly to the **left**.
choiceNotes.c: The pulmonary valve is **superior** (not inferior) and slightly to the **left** (not right) of the aortic valve.
choiceNotes.d: The pulmonary valve is **anterior**, not posterior, to the aortic valve.
choiceNotes.e: This is the position of the **aortic** valve, which is wedged centrally between the mitral and tricuspid valves.

stem: Which component of the cardiac fibrous skeleton forms a **dense junction** between the mitral and tricuspid anuli, the left ventricular–aortic junction below the noncoronary cusp, and the membranous septum?

choices.text: Left fibrous trigone
Tendon of the infundibulum
Tendon of Todaro
Right fibrous trigone
Sinutubular junction

explanation.text: The **right fibrous trigone** is the dense junction of the mitral anulus, tricuspid anulus, LV–aortic junction (below the **noncoronary** cusp) and membranous septum, and it is **pierced by the bundle of His**.

explanation.center: **Central fibrous body** (core of the fibrous skeleton)

children: More anterior and to the left
Between LV–aortic junction and mitral anulus
Joins the pulmonary valve to the central skeleton
Also joins the central fibrous body

explanation.text: The **mitral and tricuspid anuli** merge with each other and the **membranous septum** to form the fibrous skeleton; its core is the **central fibrous body** with two extensions, the right and left trigones.
Only the **right** trigone joins **both AV anuli** and is pierced by the His bundle; the **left** trigone joins only the LV–aortic junction and the **mitral** anulus.

The right fibrous trigone forms a dense junction between the mitral and tricuspid anuli, the left ventricular–aortic junction below the noncoronary cusp and the membranous septum. The trigone is pierced by the bundle of His.

choiceNotes.a: The left fibrous trigone lies **more anteriorly and to the left**, between the LV–aortic junction and the **mitral** anulus only; it does not join the tricuspid anulus.
choiceNotes.b: The tendon of the infundibulum is a fibrous band joining the **pulmonary valve** to the central cardiac skeleton.
choiceNotes.c: The tendon of Todaro joins the central fibrous body, but it is not the junction of the two AV anuli and the membranous septum.
choiceNotes.e: The sinutubular junction is a component of the aortic root, not part of the central fibrous body.

stem: Which fibrous structure joins the more superiorly placed **pulmonary valve** to the central cardiac skeleton?

choices.text: Left fibrous trigone
Right fibrous trigone
Tendon of Todaro
Membranous septum
Tendon of the infundibulum

explanation.text: The **tendon of the infundibulum** is a fibrous band that links the **pulmonary valve** (placed more superiorly) to the central cardiac skeleton.

head: Fibrous band
Joins the central fibrous body to…
rows: Joins the central fibrous body (see AV node)
explanation.caption: Two tendons that reach the central skeleton

explanation.text: The **right** and **left fibrous trigones** are the two extensions of the central fibrous body; neither is described as joining the pulmonary valve.
The pulmonary valve is **more superiorly placed** (anterior, superior and slightly to the left of the aortic valve); the **tendon of the infundibulum** links it to the central skeleton.
The tendon of the infundibulum is a fibrous band joining the more superiorly placed pulmonary valve to the central cardiac skeleton.

choiceNotes.a: The left fibrous trigone lies between the LV–aortic junction and the **mitral** anulus.
choiceNotes.b: The right fibrous trigone joins the mitral and tricuspid anuli, the LV–aortic junction and the membranous septum, not the pulmonary valve.
choiceNotes.c: The tendon of Todaro joins the central fibrous body, but it is not described as joining the pulmonary valve.
choiceNotes.d: The membranous septum merges with the AV anuli to form the fibrous skeleton; it is not the band that joins the pulmonary valve.

stem: Malalignment of the mitral leaflets causes loss of their normally large area of coaptation. Which pair correctly gives the **normal leaflet-to-orifice area relationship** and the **structure placed under undue stress** when coaptation is lost?

choices.text: Combined leaflet area equals the orifice area; the papillary muscles
Combined leaflet area is half the orifice area; the mitral anulus
Combined leaflet area is twice the orifice area; the chordae tendineae
Combined leaflet area is twice the orifice area; the aortic–mitral anulus
Combined leaflet area is three times the orifice area; the papillary muscles

explanation.text: The two mitral leaflets together have **twice the area of the orifice**, giving a large coaptation area; losing it stresses the **chordae tendineae**, which may **rupture**.

steps.text: Combined leaflet area = **2 ×** mitral orifice area
**Large area of coaptation**
steps.label: results in

steps.text: Leaflet **malalignment** -> coaptation area lost
steps.label: if

steps.text: Undue stress on **chordae tendineae** -> may **rupture**
steps.label: then

explanation.title: Why the mitral valve needs a large coaptation area

explanation.text: The mitral valve is **bicuspid**: an **anterior** (aortic, septal) and a **posterior** (mural, ventricular) leaflet, with tissue that could be called **commissural leaflets** at the commissures.
When this large area is lost because of malalignment of the leaflets, undue stress is placed on the chordae tendineae, and they may rupture.

choiceNotes.a: The source states the combined leaflet area is **twice** the orifice area, and the stressed structures are the **chordae tendineae**.
choiceNotes.b: The leaflet area is **twice**, not half, the orifice area; the source names the chordae, not the anulus.
choiceNotes.d: The ratio is correct, but the source says the stress falls on the **chordae tendineae**, which may rupture.
choiceNotes.e: The source gives a ratio of **two**, and the stressed structures are the chordae tendineae, not the papillary muscles.

stem: On the anterior mitral leaflet, a distinct ridge separates two zones. Which statement about these zones is correct?

choices.text: The clear zone is devoid of direct chordal insertions
The clear zone is the region of leaflet closure
The rough zone is devoid of direct chordal insertions
The ridge separates the anterior leaflet from the commissural tissue
The rough zone forms the base of the leaflet at the anulus

explanation.text: The ridge separates the **rough zone** (region of **closure**) from the **clear zone**, and the clear zone has **no direct chordal insertions**.

items: Relatively **smooth free margin** with few or no indentations
Base inserts on about **one-third** of the anulus

explanation.text: **Rough** = region of **closure**; **clear** = **clear of direct chordae**.
A distinct ridge separates the region of closure (rough zone) from the remaining leaflet (clear zone). The clear zone is devoid of direct chordal insertions.

choiceNotes.b: The region of closure is the **rough** zone; the clear zone is the remaining leaflet.
choiceNotes.c: It is the **clear** zone that is devoid of direct chordal insertions.
choiceNotes.d: The ridge separates the **rough** zone from the **clear** zone within the leaflet.
choiceNotes.e: The rough zone is the region of **closure**; the source does not place it at the leaflet base.

stem: Which statement correctly compares the two leaflets of the **mitral valve**?

choices.text: The anterior leaflet is smaller and inserts on about two-thirds of the anulus
The posterior leaflet is larger and inserts on about one-third of the anulus
The posterior leaflet is triangular, with a smooth free margin
The anterior leaflet is typically scalloped, with three segments
The anterior leaflet is larger and inserts on about one-third of the anulus

explanation.text: The **anterior** leaflet is the **larger** leaflet but inserts on only about **one-third** of the anulus; the smaller **posterior** leaflet inserts on about **two-thirds** and is scalloped.
Do not equate leaflet size with annular length: the **larger** anterior leaflet has the **shorter** annular attachment.
The posterior leaflet was divided into **three segments** in 46 of 50 normal mitral valves studied.
The smaller posterior (mural, ventricular, posterolateral) leaflet inserts into about two-thirds of the anulus and typically has a scalloped appearance.

choiceNotes.a: The anterior leaflet is the **larger** leaflet and inserts on about **one-third** of the anulus.
choiceNotes.b: The posterior leaflet is the **smaller** leaflet and inserts on about **two-thirds** of the anulus.
choiceNotes.c: Triangular shape with a smooth free margin describes the **anterior** leaflet.
choiceNotes.d: The **posterior** leaflet is the scalloped one, usually with three segments.

stem: The anterior mitral leaflet is in **fibrous continuity** with the aortic valve. Which description of this region of continuity is correct?

choices.text: About one-third of the mitral anulus, beneath the whole noncoronary cusp
About one-fourth of the mitral anulus, beneath half the left coronary and half the noncoronary cusp
About one-fourth of the mitral anulus, beneath half the right coronary and half the noncoronary cusp
About one-half of the mitral anulus, beneath the left coronary cusp only
About two-thirds of the mitral anulus, beneath all three aortic cusps

explanation.text: Aortic–mitral continuity occupies about **one-fourth** of the mitral anulus, beneath **half the left coronary cusp and half the noncoronary cusp**, and is limited by the **right and left fibrous trigones**.

children: Anterior leaflet forms a boundary of the **LV outflow tract**

explanation.text: The **right coronary** cusp is not above the mitral valve; the continuity lies beneath the **left coronary** and **noncoronary** cusps.
This region of continuity occupies about one-fourth of the mitral anulus and corresponds to the region beneath half the left coronary cusp and half the noncoronary cusp of the aortic valve.

choiceNotes.a: The continuity occupies about **one-fourth** of the anulus and lies beneath **half** of two cusps (left coronary and noncoronary).
choiceNotes.c: The continuity lies beneath the **left coronary** (not right coronary) and noncoronary cusps.
choiceNotes.d: The extent is about **one-fourth**, beneath half of both the left coronary and noncoronary cusps.
choiceNotes.e: About two-thirds of the mitral anulus is the share of the **posterior** leaflet; the continuity is about one-fourth.

stem: During combined aortic and mitral valve surgery, which structure lies **directly over the middle of the anterior leaflet** of the mitral valve?

choices.text: The commissure between the right and left coronary sinuses
The commissure between the right and noncoronary sinuses
One of the two commissures of the mitral valve
The commissure between the left and noncoronary sinuses
The right fibrous trigone

explanation.text: The **left–noncoronary commissure** (the posterior commissure of the aortic valve) sits **directly over the midpoint of the anterior mitral leaflet**.

Fig. 1.24A shows the same thing from the mitral side: the **posterior commissure** of the aortic valve is directly over the **midpoint of the anterior mitral leaflet**, and the **subaortic curtain** is the aortic–mitral anulus.
These aortic points **do not correspond to the commissures of the mitral valve**. The ends of the continuity are marked by the **right and left fibrous trigones**.
In Fig. 1.25A the same midpoint line divides the chordal attachments to the **anterior** and **posterior** papillary muscles.
The commissure between the left and noncoronary sinuses of the aortic valve is located directly over the middle of the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve

choiceNotes.a: The right–left commissure is not described over the mitral valve; the source names the **left–noncoronary** commissure.
choiceNotes.b: The right–noncoronary commissure overlies the region where the left bundle branch arises, not the middle of the anterior mitral leaflet.
choiceNotes.c: The source states that the aortic points above the anterior leaflet **do not correspond** to the mitral commissures.
choiceNotes.e: The fibrous trigones demarcate the **limits** (ends) of aortic–mitral continuity, not its middle.

source.loc: p. 13, Bundle of His and Bundle Branches

stem: During **mitral valve replacement**, sutures are placed deeply in the anulus **adjacent to the right fibrous trigone**. Which structures are at greatest risk of surgical damage at this site?

choices.text: The AV node and bundle of His
The sinoatrial node
The first septal branch of the left anterior descending artery
The pulmonary valve cusps
The tendon of the infundibulum

explanation.text: The **AV node and His bundle** lie at the **right fibrous trigone**, so they are at risk during mitral surgery next to this trigone.

steps.text: **Right fibrous trigone** = one limit of aortic–mitral continuity
Trigone is **pierced by the bundle of His**
steps.label: and

steps.text: **AV node and His bundle** at risk of surgical damage
steps.label: so

head: Trigone
Position
Conduction tissue
rows: Junction of mitral + tricuspid anuli, LV–aortic junction, membranous septum
More anterior and to the left; LV–aortic junction to mitral anulus
explanation.caption: Right vs left fibrous trigone

explanation.text: The AV node and His bundle are at risk of surgical damage adjacent to the right trigone.

choiceNotes.b: The sinoatrial node lies along the anterolateral aspect of the junction between the superior vena cava and the right atrial appendage, not at the mitral anulus.
choiceNotes.c: The first septal branch of the LAD pierces the septum below the **subpulmonary infundibulum**, not at the mitral anulus.
choiceNotes.d: The pulmonary valve lies anterior, superior and slightly to the left of the aortic valve; the source names the AV node and His bundle as the structures at risk next to the right trigone.
choiceNotes.e: The tendon of the infundibulum joins the pulmonary valve to the central skeleton; the source names the AV node and His bundle as the structures at risk here.

stem: Which part of the **posterior mitral leaflet** receives chordae **directly from left ventricular trabeculae**?

choices.text: The rough zone
The clear zone
The basal zone
The free edge of the middle scallop
The commissural tissue

explanation.text: The **basal zone**, close to the anulus, is unique to the **posterior** leaflet and receives chordae **directly from left ventricular trabeculae**.
Only the **posterior** leaflet has a basal zone; the anterior leaflet has only rough and clear zones.
The posterior leaflet has rough and clear zones corresponding to those of the anterior leaflet and a basal zone close to the anulus, which receives chordae directly from left ventricular trabeculae.

choiceNotes.a: The rough zone is the region of closure; it is not described as receiving chordae from trabeculae.
choiceNotes.b: The clear zone is the leaflet region beyond the closure ridge; on the anterior leaflet it has no direct chordal insertions.
choiceNotes.d: Most chordae insert on the free leaflet edge, but they arise from the **papillary muscles**, not directly from trabeculae.
choiceNotes.e: Commissural chordae arise from the **highest tip of the papillary muscle**, not directly from trabeculae.

stem: On intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography, a mitral lesion is localized to segment **P3**. Which part of the valve is this?

choices.text: The anterolateral section of the posterior leaflet
The middle section of the posterior leaflet
The posteromedial section of the anterior leaflet
The anterolateral section of the anterior leaflet
The posteromedial section of the posterior leaflet

explanation.text: **P** = posterior leaflet; **3** = posteromedial section. So **P3** is the **posteromedial section of the posterior leaflet**.
Number from **1 to 3** going from the **anterolateral** side to the **posteromedial** side; the letter names the leaflet.
This classification is used to describe morphology **at operation**, on **multiplane 2D transesophageal** echocardiography and on **3D echocardiography**.
Sections A1 and P1 represent the anterolateral sections, A2 and P2 the middle sections, and A3 and P3 the posteromedial sections.

choiceNotes.a: The anterolateral section of the posterior leaflet is **P1**.
choiceNotes.b: The middle section of the posterior leaflet is **P2**.
choiceNotes.c: The posteromedial section of the anterior leaflet is **A3**.
choiceNotes.d: The anterolateral section of the anterior leaflet is **A1**.

stem: As viewed by the surgeon through the usual **right-side approach** to the mitral valve, the **posteromedial papillary muscle** sends chordae to which portion of the leaflets?

choices.text: The left half of both the anterior and posterior leaflets
The right-sided half of both the anterior and posterior leaflets
The whole posterior leaflet only
The whole anterior leaflet only
The right half of the anterior and the left half of the posterior leaflet

explanation.text: Each leaflet receives chordae from **both** papillary muscles: the **posteromedial** muscle supplies the **right-sided half** of both leaflets, the **anterolateral** muscle the **left half** (surgeon's view).

head: Papillary muscle
Chordae go to (surgeon's right-side view)
rows: **Left half** of the anterior **and** posterior leaflets
==**Right-sided half** of the anterior **and** posterior leaflets==
explanation.caption: Papillary muscle territories

explanation.text: A papillary muscle is **not** tied to one leaflet. Each leaflet gets chordae from **both** muscles; the dividing line is the **midpoint** of both leaflets (dashed line, Fig. 1.25A).
Most chordae come from these **two large papillary muscles**, and the majority insert on the **free leaflet edge**.
the posteromedial papillary muscle is attached by chordae tendineae to the right-sided half of both anterior and posterior leaflets.

choiceNotes.a: The left half of both leaflets is the territory of the **anterolateral** papillary muscle.
choiceNotes.c: Each leaflet receives chordae from **both** papillary muscles; no papillary muscle supplies one whole leaflet.
choiceNotes.d: Each leaflet receives chordae from **both** papillary muscles; the posteromedial muscle supplies half of each leaflet.
choiceNotes.e: The posteromedial muscle supplies the **same** (right-sided) half of both leaflets.

stem: Left ventricular papillary muscles often look **fingerlike** on angiography or 2-dimensional echocardiography. Which statement about them is correct?

choices.text: They are fingerlike columns that protrude freely into the cavity
They arise from the ventricular septum rather than the free wall
Each papillary muscle sends chordae to only one leaflet
They are crescent shaped, conforming to the curvature of the free wall
Most of their chordae insert at the base of the leaflets

explanation.text: Papillary muscles are really **crescent shaped**, following the curvature of the LV **free wall**; the fingerlike look comes from **two-dimensional** imaging.

steps.text: Papillary muscles and chordae arise embryologically by **undermining of the LV myocardium**
Muscles keep a **crescent shape** that conforms to the **free wall** curvature
steps.label: so

steps.text: 2D angiography or echo shows them as **fingerlike** projections
steps.label: but

explanation.text: They are described as an **anterolateral group** and a **posteromedial group**, because there is often more than one muscle **belly**.
Actually, the papillary muscles have a somewhat crescent shape that conforms to the curvature of the free wall of the left ventricle.

choiceNotes.a: The fingerlike appearance comes from viewing them in **two dimensions**; their real shape is crescentic.
choiceNotes.b: The source describes them as conforming to the curvature of the **free wall** of the left ventricle.
choiceNotes.c: Each leaflet receives chordae from **both** papillary muscles, so each muscle supplies both leaflets.
choiceNotes.e: The majority of chordae insert on the **free leaflet edge**.

stem: In a left ventricular papillary muscle group with **three muscle bellies**, which feature is described?

choices.text: The belly supporting the commissural chordae arises separately from the ventricular wall
The belly supporting the commissural chordae arises from the ventricular septum
The commissural chordae are the longest chordae of the valve
The commissural chordae arise from the base of the papillary muscle
Each belly supports chordae to the anterior leaflet only

explanation.text: With **three bellies**, the belly carrying the **commissural** chordae **arises separately from the ventricular wall**.

children: Usually the **highest tip** of the papillary muscle
Supporting belly arises **separately** from the ventricular wall

explanation.text: Bellies are mostly **one or two**, occasionally **three, four or even five**. Usually **4 to 12** chordae originate from each papillary muscle group.
When there are three muscle bellies, the papillary muscle supporting the chordae to the commissure arises separately from the ventricular wall.

choiceNotes.b: The source says it arises separately from the **ventricular wall**; the septum is not mentioned.
choiceNotes.c: Commissural chordae are **shorter** than the others.
choiceNotes.d: Commissural chordae usually originate from the **highest tip** of the papillary muscle.
choiceNotes.e: Each leaflet receives chordae from both papillary muscle groups; the bellies are not limited to the anterior leaflet.

stem: In the clinical morphologic classification of papillary muscles, which description corresponds to a **Type II** papillary muscle?

choices.text: A single undivided papillary muscle
Cleaved in a coronal plane, forming an individual head that supports the commissural chordae
Cleaved in a sagittal plane into two heads that separately support the anterior and posterior leaflets
Divided into multiple heads, with a separate band near the anulus supporting short commissural chordae
Cleaved in a coronal plane into two heads that separately support the anterior and posterior leaflets

explanation.text: **Type II** = cleaved in a **sagittal** plane into **two heads**, one for the **anterior** and one for the **posterior** leaflet.

head: Type
Morphology
What it supports
rows: Cleaved in a **sagittal** plane into two heads
An individual head for the **commissural** chordae
**Multiple** heads + separate band close to the mitral anulus
explanation.caption: Clinical morphologic classification of papillary muscles

explanation.text: **S**agittal splits the **S**upport between the two leaflets (Type II); **C**oronal carves out a **C**ommissural head (Type III).
Type II refers to papillary muscles cleaved in a sagittal plane into two heads that separately support the anterior and posterior leaflets of the mitral valve.

choiceNotes.a: A single undivided papillary muscle is **Type I**.
choiceNotes.b: A coronal cleft forming a head for the commissural chordae is **Type III**.
choiceNotes.d: Multiple heads with a separate band near the anulus is **Type IV**.
choiceNotes.e: Separate heads for the anterior and posterior leaflets come from a **sagittal** (not coronal) cleft.

stem: Chordae tendineae are classified into three orders by their site of insertion. Which statement about **third-order chordae** is correct?

choices.text: They insert on the free margin of the leaflet
They insert a few to several millimeters back from the free edge
They insert at the base of both mitral leaflets equally
They arise from the highest tip of the papillary muscle
They insert at the base of the leaflet and apply only to the posterior leaflet

explanation.text: **Third-order** chordae insert at the **base** of the leaflet, and this applies **only to the posterior leaflet**.

head: Order
Insertion site
rows: A few to several mm **back from the free edge**

choiceNotes.b: Insertion a few to several millimeters back from the free edge defines **second-order** chordae.
choiceNotes.c: Third-order chordae apply **only to the posterior** leaflet.

stem: During diastolic filling, the mitral valve opens as the anterior leaflet swings anteriorly away from the posterior leaflet. Which additional mechanism **enhances the orifice dimensions**?

choices.text: Shortening of the commissural chordae
Flexion of the anterior leaflet
Folding of the posterior leaflet scallops
Stretching of the aortic–mitral anulus
Contraction of the papillary muscles

explanation.text: Orifice dimensions are enhanced by **flexion of the anterior leaflet** as it opens (the flexion lines in Fig. 1.25B).

steps.text: **Diastole**: low pressures in LA and LV
Anterior leaflet **swings anteriorly** away from the posterior leaflet
steps.label: valve opens

steps.text: Anterior leaflet **flexes**
steps.label: and

steps.text: **Widest possible orifice**, least obstruction to flow
steps.label: result

explanation.text: The mitral design gives the **largest possible orifice** in diastole and limits even the slightest obstruction to flow at **low pressures**.
The valve opens as the anterior leaflet swings anteriorly away from the posterior leaflet. Orifice dimensions are enhanced by flexion of the anterior leaflet

choiceNotes.a: The source does not describe chordal shortening as an opening mechanism; it names **flexion of the anterior leaflet**.
choiceNotes.c: The source attributes the enlarged orifice to the **anterior** leaflet flexing, not to the posterior leaflet.
choiceNotes.d: The aortic–mitral anulus is not described as stretching in diastole; the mechanism is anterior leaflet flexion.
choiceNotes.e: Papillary muscle contraction is not given as the mechanism; the source names **flexion of the anterior leaflet**.

stem: During systole, the mitral valve closes under the full load of left ventricular contraction while the anterior leaflet straightens and extends toward the posterior leaflet. What is the role of the **posterior leaflet** as the leaflets appose?

choices.text: It swings anteriorly to widen the orifice
It flexes to create the widest possible orifice
It extends toward the aortic valve to close the outflow tract
It acts like a shelf that stops the movement of the anterior leaflet
It separates into commissural leaflets to seal the commissures

explanation.text: In systole the **posterior leaflet acts like a shelf**: it **stops** the moving anterior leaflet as the leaflets appose.

head: Phase
Anterior leaflet
Posterior leaflet
rows: **Straightens** and extends toward the posterior leaflet
explanation.caption: Leaflet roles through the cardiac cycle

explanation.text: The anterior leaflet is the **door**; the posterior leaflet is the **shelf (door stop)** it closes against.
The anterior leaflet straightens and extends toward the posterior leaflet. The posterior leaflet functions like a shelf to stop the movement of the anterior leaflet as the leaflets appose.

choiceNotes.a: Swinging anteriorly to open the valve is what the **anterior** leaflet does in **diastole**.
choiceNotes.b: Flexion to create the widest orifice is a **diastolic** action of the **anterior** leaflet.
choiceNotes.c: The source describes the **anterior** leaflet extending toward the posterior leaflet; the posterior leaflet is the stop.
choiceNotes.e: Commissural leaflet tissue is not described as having this role; the posterior leaflet acts as a **shelf**.

stem: Which feature of the **tricuspid valve**, compared with the mitral valve, is correct?

choices.text: Its orifice is roughly triangular and larger than the mitral orifice
Its anulus is distinct, especially in the septal region
Its leaflets and chordae are thicker than those of the mitral valve
Its orientation is nearly horizontal
Its orifice is smaller than the mitral orifice

explanation.text: The tricuspid orifice is **roughly triangular** and **larger** than the mitral orifice.
The tricuspid anulus is **least distinct in the septal region**, the opposite of a "distinct septal anulus".
Its orifice is roughly triangular and larger than the mitral orifice. The anulus is relatively indistinct, especially in the septal region.

choiceNotes.b: The tricuspid anulus is relatively **indistinct**, especially in the septal region.
choiceNotes.c: Tricuspid leaflets and chordae are **thinner** than those of the mitral valve.
choiceNotes.d: The tricuspid valve orientation is nearly **vertical**.
choiceNotes.e: The tricuspid orifice is **larger** than the mitral orifice.

stem: During tricuspid valve repair, a deep notch is found in the **anterior leaflet close to the anteroseptal commissure**. How can it be differentiated from a true commissure?

choices.text: By its depth, because a notch is always shallow
By the presence of a fibrous nodule at its base
By the type of chordal attachments
By its attachment to the membranous septum
By its position relative to the coronary sinus

explanation.text: A notch in the anterior leaflet can be as deep as a commissure; it is told apart from a **true commissure** by the **type of chordal attachments**.

children: Notch near the **anteroseptal commissure** in 47 of 50 leaflets
Base from RV free wall and **TSM**

explanation.text: Depth does **not** help: the notch was **occasionally as deep as a commissure**.
This notch was occasionally as deep as a commissure but could be differentiated from a true commissure by the type of chordal attachments.

choiceNotes.a: The notch was occasionally **as deep as a commissure**, so depth does not separate them.
choiceNotes.b: A fibrous nodule at the midpoint of the free edge is a feature of **semilunar** valve cusps, not a way to identify tricuspid commissures.
choiceNotes.d: Attachments to the membranous septum are variable (parts of either the septal or the anterior leaflet may attach there); the source separates a notch from a commissure by its **chordal attachments**.
choiceNotes.e: The coronary sinus is not used in the source to identify tricuspid commissures.

stem: A tricuspid leaflet receives its chordae from the **posterior and anterior papillary muscles** and is attached **wholly to the right ventricular free wall**. Which leaflet is it, and what is its usual size?

choices.text: Septal leaflet; usually the smallest
Anterior leaflet; the largest
Septal leaflet; slightly larger than the posterior leaflet
Posterior leaflet; the largest
Posterior leaflet; usually the smallest

explanation.text: The **posterior (inferior)** leaflet: usually the **smallest**, commonly **scalloped**, chordae from the **posterior and anterior** papillary muscles, attached **wholly to the free wall**.
"Wholly to the free wall" rules out the septal leaflet, which attaches mostly to the ventricular septum.

The posterior (inferior) leaflet is usually the smallest and is commonly scalloped. Its chordae originate from the posterior and anterior papillary muscles. It is attached wholly to the ventricular free wall.

choiceNotes.a: The septal leaflet is usually **slightly larger** than the posterior leaflet, and it attaches mostly to the **septum**.
choiceNotes.b: The anterior leaflet receives chordae from the **anterior and medial** papillary muscles.
choiceNotes.c: The septal leaflet receives chordae from the **posterior and septal** papillary muscles and attaches mostly to the septum.
choiceNotes.d: The posterior leaflet is usually the **smallest**; the anterior leaflet is the largest.

stem: Which statement about the **septal leaflet** of the tricuspid valve is correct?

choices.text: It is attached wholly to the right ventricular free wall
Its chordae arise from the posterior and septal papillary muscles
It is the largest of the three tricuspid leaflets
Its chordae arise from the anterior and medial papillary muscles
It never attaches to the posterior wall of the right ventricle

explanation.text: The **septal leaflet** receives chordae from the **posterior and septal** papillary muscles.

children: Usually **slightly larger** than the posterior leaflet
Part may attach to the **posterior RV wall**
At the transition from posterior wall to septum

explanation.text: The **posterior** papillary muscle feeds two leaflets: the **posterior** leaflet (with the anterior PM) and the **septal** leaflet (with the septal PM).
The septal leaflet is usually slightly larger than the posterior leaflet. Its chordae arise from the posterior and septal papillary muscles.

choiceNotes.a: Wholly free-wall attachment describes the **posterior** leaflet; the septal leaflet attaches mostly to the septum.
choiceNotes.c: The **anterior** leaflet is the largest; the septal leaflet is only slightly larger than the posterior.
choiceNotes.d: Chordae from the anterior and medial papillary muscles go to the **anterior** leaflet.
choiceNotes.e: Part of the septal leaflet **may attach to the posterior wall** of the right ventricle, with a fold at the transition.

stem: Of major surgical importance in tricuspid valve operations is the proximity of the conduction system to the septal leaflet. Where is the **bundle of His** usually found relative to the tricuspid **anteroseptal commissure**?

choices.text: At the base of the anterior papillary muscle of the right ventricle
Within the anterior leaflet, about 5 mm superior to the anteroseptal commissure
Along the attachment of the posterior leaflet to the free wall
Beneath the interventricular membranous septum, about 5 mm inferior to the anteroseptal commissure
At the junction of the superior vena cava and the right atrial appendage

explanation.text: The His bundle penetrates the right trigone **beneath the interventricular component of the membranous septum**, usually **about 5 mm inferior to the anteroseptal commissure**.

steps.text: **Anteroseptal commissure** of the tricuspid valve
**Membranous septum** (usually beneath the septal leaflet)
steps.label: inferior to it

steps.text: His bundle penetrates the **right trigone** (about **5 mm** below the commissure)
steps.label: beneath its interventricular part

steps.text: Runs along the **crest of the muscular septum**
steps.label: then

explanation.title: Danger zone near the septal leaflet

explanation.text: Of **major surgical importance**: the conduction system lies close to the **septal leaflet** and its **anteroseptal commissure**.
The bundle of His penetrates the right trigone beneath the interventricular component of the membranous septum (usually about 5 mm inferior to the commissure)

choiceNotes.a: The base of the anterior papillary muscle is where the **right bundle branch** ends, not where the His bundle penetrates the trigone.
choiceNotes.b: The His bundle lies **inferior** to the commissure, beneath the membranous septum, not within the anterior leaflet.
choiceNotes.c: The posterior leaflet is attached to the free wall, away from the septal conduction tissue.
choiceNotes.e: The superior vena cava–right atrial appendage junction is the site of the **sinus node**.

source.loc: p. 13, Bundle of His and Bundle Branches

stem: The portion of the tricuspid **septal leaflet** between the membranous septum and the anteroseptal commissure extends around the anulus, away from the septum, to the right ventricular free wall. What is its surgical significance?

choices.text: It may form a flap over some VSDs
It contains the atrioventricular node
It is pierced by the first septal branch of the LAD
It forms the tendon of Todaro
It is in fibrous continuity with the pulmonary valve

explanation.text: This part of the septal leaflet **may form a flap over some VSDs**.

steps.text: Septal leaflet between **membranous septum** and **anteroseptal commissure**
Extends around the tricuspid anulus to the **RV free wall**
steps.label: away from the septum

steps.text: May form a **flap over some VSDs**
steps.label: so

explanation.text: Attachments of the septal and anterior leaflets are **variable**, so parts of **either** may attach to the membranous septum.
This portion of the tricuspid valve may form a flap over some VSDs.

choiceNotes.b: The AV node lies on the right atrial side of the right trigone, in the muscular AV septum within the triangle of Koch, not in a tricuspid leaflet.
choiceNotes.c: The first septal branch of the LAD pierces the septum below the **subpulmonary infundibulum**.
choiceNotes.d: The tendon of Todaro is the continuation of the **eustachian valve** running to the central fibrous body.
choiceNotes.e: The pulmonary valve normally **lacks** fibrous continuity with the anterior tricuspid leaflet; its cusps are supported entirely by freestanding musculature.

stem: Which statement about the structure of an **aortic valve cusp** is correct?

choices.text: The free edge is thinner and weaker than the rest of the cusp
The lunulae are thick fibrous areas at the base of the cusp
A fibrous nodulus Arantii lies at the midpoint of each free edge
Fenestrations of the lunulae occur mainly at the cusp midpoint
The area of coaptation lies at the base of the cusp near the anulus

explanation.text: Each aortic cusp has a fibrous **nodulus Arantii** at the **midpoint of its free edge**, with a thin crescent-shaped **lunula** on either side.

children: **Tougher** than the rest of the cusp
At the **midpoint** of each free edge
On either side of the nodulus
The lunular regions form it on closure

explanation.text: Lunular fenestrations are found **near the commissures**, not at the cusp midpoint (where the nodulus is).
At the midpoint of each free edge is a fibrous nodulus Arantii. On either side of each nodulus is an extremely thin, crescent-shaped portion of the cusp termed the lunula

choiceNotes.a: The free edge is of **tougher** consistency than the remainder of the cusp.
choiceNotes.b: The lunulae are **extremely thin**, crescent-shaped portions on either side of the nodulus.
choiceNotes.d: The lunulae are occasionally fenestrated **near the commissures**.
choiceNotes.e: The thin **lunulae** beside each nodulus, at the free edge, form the area of coaptation.

stem: A surgeon is planning a **proximal aortotomy**. Which property of the **aortic sinuses** makes them an important consideration?

choices.text: Their walls are considerably thicker than the wall of the aorta proper
The coronary arteries arise from all three sinuses
They are in fibrous continuity with the posterior mitral leaflet
They lie within the subpulmonary infundibulum
Their walls are considerably thinner than the wall of the aorta proper

explanation.text: The sinus walls are **considerably thinner than the aorta proper**, which matters when designing **proximal aortotomies**.

children: Outer part of the three **cuplike** closing structures

explanation.text: Thin sinus walls -> plan the proximal aortotomy with this in mind.
The walls of the sinuses are considerably thinner than the wall of the aorta proper, an important consideration when designing proximal aortotomies.

choiceNotes.a: The sinus walls are considerably **thinner**, not thicker, than the aorta proper.
choiceNotes.b: The coronary arteries arise from **two** of the aortic sinuses; the third is the noncoronary sinus.
choiceNotes.c: The aortic valve is in fibrous continuity with the **anterior** mitral leaflet.
choiceNotes.d: The subpulmonary infundibulum supports the **pulmonary** valve, not the aortic sinuses.

stem: During systole, the three-cusp aortic valve opens **widely without its cusps touching the aortic wall**. Which structures make this possible?

choices.text: The fibrous trigones
The sinuses of Valsalva
The sinutubular junction
The lunulae
The noduli Arantii

explanation.text: The **sinuses of Valsalva** let the open cusps stand away from the aortic wall, so the valve opens widely **without touching the wall** (Fig. 1.25B).

head: Root component
Part it plays
rows: ==Dilated pockets== behind the cusps; outer part of the cuplike closing structures
Delicate cusps; with the sinuses they form three **cuplike** structures
Share the coordinated action of the root
explanation.caption: Aortic root components

explanation.text: Anulus, trigones, cusps, sinuses and sinutubular junction act **together** to give **laminar flow, minimal resistance, optimal coronary flow** and **least damage to blood elements**.
Three-cusp semilunar aortic valve opens widely during systole without touching aortic wall, owing to sinuses of Valsalva.
explanation.ref: Chapter 1: Anatomy and Dimensions, p. 16, Fig. 1.25

choiceNotes.a: The fibrous trigones take part in the root's coordinated action, but the source credits the **sinuses** for keeping the open cusps off the wall.
choiceNotes.c: The sinutubular junction is part of the root, but Fig. 1.25B credits the **sinuses of Valsalva**.
choiceNotes.d: The lunulae are thin crescent-shaped coaptation areas of the cusp, not the space behind it.
choiceNotes.e: The noduli Arantii are fibrous nodules at the midpoint of each free edge, not the reason the cusps avoid the wall.

stem: The pulmonary valve structure is similar to that of the aortic valve. Which is a normal feature that **distinguishes the pulmonary valve** from the aortic valve?

choices.text: Three cusps, each with a nodule at the midpoint of the free edge
Lunulae on both sides of each nodule
A sinus in the pocket behind each cusp
Lack of fibrous continuity with the anterior tricuspid leaflet
Heavier construction of the cusps

explanation.text: A **normal lack of fibrous continuity** with the **anterior tricuspid leaflet** is one of the three major differences of the pulmonary valve from the aortic valve.

head: Feature
Aortic valve
Pulmonary valve
rows: Fibrous continuity with an AV valve
explanation.caption: Three major differences (highlighted)

explanation.text: **L-A-N** for the pulmonary valve: **L**ighter cusps, **A**bsent coronaries, **N**o fibrous continuity.

Major differences from the aortic valve are (1) lighter construction of pulmonary valve cusps, (2) normal absence of coronary artery origins, and (3) normal lack of fibrous continuity with the anterior tricuspid valve leaflet.

choiceNotes.a: Three cusps with a nodule at the midpoint of each free edge are **shared** with the aortic valve.
choiceNotes.b: Lunulae on both sides of the nodules are **shared** with the aortic valve.
choiceNotes.c: A sinus behind each cusp is **shared** with the aortic valve.
choiceNotes.e: Pulmonary cusps are of **lighter** construction than aortic cusps.

stem: The pulmonary valve cusps are supported entirely by freestanding musculature and are lifted away from the ventricular septum by the **subpulmonary infundibulum**. Which artery pierces the ventricular septum **below the shortest part** of this infundibulum?

choices.text: The first septal branch of the left anterior descending artery
The first diagonal branch of the left anterior descending artery
The posterior descending artery
The first obtuse marginal branch of the circumflex artery
The sinus node artery

explanation.text: The **first septal branch of the LAD** pierces the septum **below the shortest part of the subpulmonary infundibulum**, which protects it.

steps.text: **Pulmonary valve cusps**
**Subpulmonary infundibulum** (freestanding musculature)
steps.label: supported entirely by

steps.text: **First septal branch of the LAD** pierces the septum
steps.label: below its shortest part

explanation.title: From valve down to the septal artery

explanation.text: Pulmonary cusps have **no direct relationship with the ventricular septum**: the infundibulum lifts the valve away from it and **protects** the first septal artery.

The first septal branch of the left anterior descending coronary artery pierces the ventricular septum below the shortest part of the subpulmonary infundibulum. The artery is protected by the subpulmonary infundibulum.

choiceNotes.b: Diagonal branches of the LAD supply the **anterior portion of the left ventricle**; the source names the **first septal** branch here.
choiceNotes.c: The posterior descending artery encircles the septum **behind**, forming the posterior part of the loop.
choiceNotes.d: Obtuse marginal branches stream down the **back of the left ventricle**.
choiceNotes.e: The sinus node artery pierces the **sinus node**, not the ventricular septum.

stem: A commissure of the pulmonary valve was found adjacent to a commissure of the aortic valve in 199 of 200 specimens. Based on this relationship, which terminology was suggested for the cusps of **each arterial valve**?

choices.text: Right coronary, left coronary, and noncoronary
Right, left, and anterior (nonseptal)
Right adjacent, left adjacent, and opposite
Anterior, posterior, and septal
Anterolateral, middle, and posteromedial

explanation.text: Because the two arterial valves have **adjacent commissures**, their cusps can be named **right adjacent, left adjacent and opposite** (or **right facing, left facing and nonfacing**).

head: Naming system
Cusp names
Used for
rows: Usual pulmonary names (relation to the aortic valve)
explanation.caption: Cusp nomenclatures

explanation.text: **Adjacent = facing**: right adjacent = right facing, left adjacent = left facing, opposite = nonfacing.
These investigators suggested that the cusps of each arterial valve should be termed right adjacent, left adjacent, and opposite

choiceNotes.a: Naming by the coronary ostia applies to the **aortic** sinuses and cusps only, since the pulmonary valve normally has no coronary origins.
choiceNotes.b: Right, left and anterior (nonseptal) are the **usual** pulmonary cusp names, based on their relation to the aortic valve, not the adjacent-commissure terminology.
choiceNotes.d: Anterior, posterior and septal are the leaflets of the **tricuspid** valve.
choiceNotes.e: Anterolateral, middle and posteromedial are the sections of the **mitral** segmental classification.
